reviews.review_text: leigh bardugo writes it, i read it.for better or worse.guess which one it is in this case.welcome to THE FAMILIAR, the genre-bending, worst-of-both-worlds historical fantasy universe of luzia. luzia is a maid. she is also magic. she is also boring.luzia is an orphan who works in some middle class evil lady's house cleaning stuff all day. she is obsessed with her aunt, who has a lot of money. you may be like "why doesn't she live with her aunt, then?" because she is a kept woman. you might then wonder why luzia's girlboss self is so bothered by this: she is not. she sleeps on a dusty floor instead of on, like, glamorous cushions with her dear family member because her (dead) dad thought her aunt's reputation was bad and that's the worst thing that can happen to a girl. the concept of being near a bad reputation. because of wanting to get married.do not dwell on that too long, because we're going to ignore it for the rest of the plot.we're hot in the middle of the SPANISH GOLDEN AGE, and it's evil to be a witch but it's very rad to be so christian it actually makes you magic. luzia sets off to participate in a god's love contest, along with her abusive employer (ignore that), her aunt's bad reputation (ignore that), a million year old creep (ignore that, he's supposed to suddenly become sexy), her aunt's boyfriend and his wife (ignore that), and a few ragtag others.discerning readers may remember we mentioned a creepy ancient man we are supposed to find unbelievably hot about halfway through. this wannabe edward cullen makes up half of the world's most soulless romance.somehow i'm reading about magical star-crossed lovers and their doomed soulmate status but i know couples from my high school whose stories i'm more interested in. which is maybe not a fair comparison because i love gossip, but still.on top of being a boring romance, this is not a convincing historical fiction. that doesn't bother me really (i hate reading modern writers try to write old-timey), but the fact that it's also not a convincing teller of its own story does.this book is not sure how our protagonist knows so much, or expects more for herself, or practices her magic. it kind of just inconsistently provides her with whatever is convenient for the scraps of plot we're navigating and hopes we don't have follow-up questions or memory of what we've already read.the writing, too, is style-first: sentences sound good, but when you take away the drama, they don't really fit together. the sweeping gestures of characters and of wording...both of them rarely make sense.also, for some reason our narrator is omnipotent.yes. all of the side characters' internal thoughts and feelings pop up from time to time like an annoying bug, seeming like a shallow afterthought compared to the protagonist's, with none of it going beyond what you or the main character would assume. so why bother? who knows!that's not the only perspective choice that left me shaking my damn head either. to have it be speaking from the future and casting opinions on the events of the story was even weirder. it's so annoying to be like "perhaps if luzia had gotten a haircut that day everything would be different." ok butterfly effect!i can always tell i really didn't like a book if i have multiple paragraphs' worth of thoughts about a single writing element. but i force myself to digress.in the most annoying and present sin of all, this is not a story of magic trials and sorcery.it's about old-timey european politics.the climax occurs when a former secretary loses his job.unforgivable.bottom line: this book is nothing that it said it was, and nothing that it wanted to be, and nothing when you dig into it at all.

The Familiaris a perfectly adequate book. The prose is serviceable. The character motivations make sense. The historical setting is carefully rendered. In fact, had it been a debut novel written by an up-and-coming author, I would have praised its well constructed—if a little predictable—plot and overlooked the simplicity with which the themes are presented.But this wasn’t written by just any author. It was written by Leigh Bardugo, a literary powerhouse who could publish her shopping list and turn it into an instant bestseller. I’ve loved some of Bardugo’s past works and heavily disliked some others, but this is the first time I feel absolutely neutral about one of her books.My feelings are probably due to the fact that nearly everything aboutThe Familiarfeels generic: the underdog female protagonist who looks plain and unremarkable, but is in fact extremely powerful; the shallow feminist message that the narrative beats you over the head with; and, of course, the shoehorned romance between a virginal young woman and a brooding immortal man. Groundbreaking.I kept waiting for something to awaken my interest and set this story apart from the hundreds of romantasy novels that populate the shelves of book stores everywhere; but alas, that something never came. Even Bardugo’s writing style, which is usually one of her stronger assets, felt bland here. There was no trace of her signature irony and wit in the dialogue, no memorable line that stood out to me.The characters read less like human beings and more like archetypes that the author employs to develop a plot point or drive home a certain message. Every single male character apart from the love interest is thoroughly unlikeable and misogynistic; the commentary on class and religious persecution feels very obvious and repetitive. Given that this author is known for writing layered and compelling villains, I was disappointed with how cartoonishly evil the antagonist acted right from the start.Most of all, I was underwhelmed by the romance. The two leads seemed to have nothing in common apart from their magic, and I was puzzled by how quickly they went from barely knowing each other to being madly in love. Santangel in particular was utterly charmless and far from the twisted, dangerous demon that everyone in the book seemed to think he was.WithNinth House, Bardugo proved that she was willing to experiment with her fiction; that she could write darker, grittier, more complex stories presenting thorny themes in a nuanced manner. None of that complexity made it to this book. This is a paint-by-numbers historical fantasy, virtually indistinguishable from the plethora of similar stories published in the past five years to chase the latest trends and appeal to the widest possible audience. I am frankly disappointed that this is all Bardugo could come up with when presented with an opportunity to write literally whatever she wanted.

But this story has a lot of heart, and a lot of tragedy, and you can really tell leigh put a lot of her soul in this story. this book takes place in madrid, during spain’s golden age - where spain colonized, forced labor, forced religious oppression, and forced cultural assimilation (i say this as a filipino, while also recognizing maybe this hit a little bit harder because of my family). but this is also a historical fantasy about three women and an immortal, all cursed in their own ways, all trying to survive in this world that constantly tries to silence them.➛ Valentina -forced to ask her husband for permission to even leave her house, while also trying to present a fake front of wealth to the upper class society, despite not having much wealth anymore. Valentina is very desperate to gain some kind of agency, and attention from the upper class, and sees a way to do both when she notices a housemaid able to perform magic. but gaining the attention of more powerful eyes might not be a good thing for anyone.➛ Luzia -works for valentina as a housemaid, and is able to perform magic because of her jewish ancestry she has always been forced to keep secret from the world. but because of valentina, her secret has now spread, and she soon has a tournament to win, for a wealthy patron who wants to gain the attention of the king, who wants to keep winning his wars. luzia is forced to walk the line of performing magic that will please, but not magic that will scare her oppressors forcing her to perform said magic.➛ Santángel -the immortal (points you to title) who is tasked with helping train luzia to win the competition, but who also has a lot of secrets and mystery from his own past, that keeps haunting him lifetime after lifetime.➛ Hualit -luzia’s aunt, whose story really intrigued me because she has lived her life doing everything she thinks was needed to survive. i would say that her storyline is the smallest of the four, but she impacted me so much that she needed her own bullet point!and i really love all four of these very complex characters, very deeply! “Because it is a language that spends its power in command and conquest. But you were wrong when you said you didn’t need the words. You do need them. Just as God did when He set this whole miserable clockwork running. Language creates possibility. Sometimes by being used. Sometimes by being kept secret.”Wow. Without a doubt, will be one of my favorites of the year. Dazzling, quietly perseverant, and captivating, THE FAMILIAR is a testament to resilience. It’s a testament to the Jewish experience. It’s a testament to survival–to protecting the most precious parts of ourselves for ourselves however we must.There’s something that gets me choked up about reading Jewish stories that center this particular brand of resistance: the kind that isn’t about changing the world, but is about taking care of ourselves and each other. Of course, Jewish revolution and political action can be just as moving, but for so much of our history, we did have to put our heads down and keep our communities safe through quieted whispers and clenched teeth and clasped palms. Through keeping the most valuable parts of our identities close to our chest. And this isn’t a story about moving the political tide or making waves in the minds of the masses towards acceptance. It’s a story about drops in the water and the ripple effect they can make. It’s about perseverance through preservation. And there’s something so preciously Jewish about that. (Honestly it makes me want to cry just thinking about it.)The characters here are all so brilliant and riveting. Luzia is fierce and bull-headed and daring, everything I love in a strong female protagonist. Valentina is brave, stumbling into her own self-discovery. But I think my favorite was Santángel, who felt like a cross between Ariel from the Tempest and Erik (the Phantom) from The Phantom of the Opera, with a sprinkling of Howl from Howl’s Moving Castle. But as all good characters should, their individual traits truly shine when they come into contact with each other, molding and scarring each other for the better.I know many people will walk away from this book simping over the love interest or gushing over the romance, and honestly, I get it, I am a little bit as well. But, if I could have one hope as this goes into the world, it would be that people remember that the context of this book was very real. That the Spanish Inquisition was real. That the struggles these characters face were real struggles that Jewish and Muslim and other marginalized people faced at this time. "Witchcraft” accusations were a tool of more than just misogyny. They were a tool of empire and cultural erasure. Before the witch hunters came for the women, they came for the queer and disabled people. Before the witch hunters came for the queer and disabled people, they came for the Jews, the Muslims, the Black and Indigenous people.I think this book does an incredible job of explaining how marginalized people were targeted by this empirical effort, so I’ll just leave this quote here with you:After hundreds of years, if there were so many sinners left, what had the Inquisition accomplished? They might root out Jews and Muslims and Erasmists and alumbrados, but then what was left? The machine had been built to consume heresy and impiety, so would it simply keep finding heresy and impiety to feed on?I can’t wait for this book to launch its way out into the world and for you all to join me in this world of scorching flames, blinding jewels, and heart-softening orange blossoms. An utter masterpiece from Bardugo, THE FAMILIAR will be praised for years to come.Thank you so much to the publisher for sending me an ARC of this book in exchange for an honest review!CW: antisemitism, religious bigotry, forced assimilation, violence, blood & gore, body horror, imprisonment, torture, fire, drowning, character death, grief, misogyny, animal death, alcohol, emesis, sexual content, death of parents (past), sexual assault (past, brief)

Actual rating: 2.5.I told myself I didn't need to write a full review for this one since I'm sure everyone's going to read this book anyway, but I couldn't stop once I started. So here you go. 😂✅This book is so smartly written.You can always tell with Leigh Bardugo that her books are well thought-out. Everything makes sense and nothing seems out of place. The magic system is not really unique, but it fits well with the story and the setting and the characters. There's also just a biiit of mystery (though predictable) to keep us on our toes.❌This is one of theslowestfantasy books I've ever read.It took me 3 or 4 days just to get through the first 30% alone. The next 30% - 40% also dragged on for ages, but at least there was some build up there. It wasn't until the last 70% or so where things finally sped up and we got some good action.❓I LIKED Luzia, but I didn't necessarily love her.She's a perfect fairytale heroine -- shy and afraid at first, but then grows into a tough cookie. She's intelligent and fierce, and she knows what she wants. I just wanted more emotion from her -- it was hard to form a connection with this MC (and the rest of the characters, really).❓I don't know how to feel about Santángel.He's in the story A LOT (obviously), but I felt so disconnected from him. He felt like a ghost most of the time -- he kept randomly disappearing and appearing like some kind of Slenderman-magician hybrid (this is genuinely how I picture him). **2.5-stars rounded up**This could be me. It could be. Nevertheless, I still felt bored and admittedly, my mind wandered a lot.Our main protagonist is Luzia, who works as a scullion in the kitchen of a manor home. Luzia has magical powers, although she's never been formally trained in how to use them properly, or harness their full potential.These powers are noticed by her mistress, Valentina, who then comes up with a scheme to use Luzia's powers to gain prestige, favors and power for herself within Madrid's upper-class society.She trots Luzia out in front of her guests and makes her perform parlor tricks. Luzia ends up coming to the attention of a man connected to the King. She then gets invited to compete in a competition that could result in her being employed by the King himself.From that point, Luzia's life becomes a whirlwind. She begins magic training and enters the competition, which pits her against individuals with all sorts of different abilities.There's a bit of romance, palace intrigue and lots of interpersonal drama. Luzia's Aunt is involved, and of course her mistress, Valentina, who is the one who got her involved in this whole business in the first place.For me, the competition, which should have been my favorite aspect of this book, wasn't developed, or utilized, as much as it could have been. I know there were stakes involved, but they didn't feel high or present enough.I also felt like the magic system could have been more clear and developed as well. I would've been happy to do away with the forced romance, in order to then spend that time leaning into the darker sides of the magical elements.I think this missed an opportunity to create an unsettling, or dangerous, atmosphere. I'm not sure and at this point, we'll never find out, because I'm certainly not reading it again.With this being said, I know that Bardugo is an exceptional writer and my opinion certainly is by no means trying to negate that fact. The Familiar is a book that kept alternating between losing and gaining my trust.I think I'm in the minority in saying that the beginning hooked me immediately. Something I've always appreciated about Bardugo's writing is her dedication to always pushing her craft; The Familiar is rich, sumptuous, bitter, and sweet, leaning into the kind of luscious prose I associate with Erin Morgenstern and The Invisible Life of Addie LaRue. Luzia is an intriguing main character - witty with a bit of viciousness - and I appreciated how the narrative unfolded to encompass a larger cast. All of the characters here are a bit morally 'complicated,' but this is refreshing in a story that easily could have turned saccharine.But I struggled a bit during the middle of the story. I wasn't tempted to DNF, but The Familiar is a slow-paced (if consistent) book, and that occasionally morphed into a drag. It's also a surprisingly tropey book. If you peel back the prose, the heavily-researched (though slightly sparse) setting, the themes of resistance and ambition (brilliantly done), this is a story many readers are overly familiar with. Young poor woman's power is discovered, she enters a competition to prove her skills, she falls into a romance with a dubious bad boy... There was a hollowness at the center of this portion of this story that I had a hard time identifying, but I think this is it.But the end of the book got me again. Once Bardugo departs from the tournament-style structure, she's free to bring her characters somewhere new and expand on the ideas established in the beginning. The ending is immensely satisfying, drawing together romance, history, and fantasy into a final 60 pages I couldn't put down. The Familiar is Leigh Bardugo just being classic Leigh Bardugo, take that as you will. If you crave stories about shadow magic, overlooked women, brooding men, and the way everyone is just caught up in the games of fate, then you are likely to enjoy her latest book.It is a story of opulence and greed. And The Familiar is also the classic story of a chosen one, a diamond in the rough discovered and polished to a shine by a group of benefactors hoping to each gain from her success in a public competition comprised of three trials. All of this is set against the backdrop of the Spanish Inquisition.The writing is overwrought, syrupy and lush while the dialogue cuts, wit and condescension slicing through the prose. The contrasts are stark and the characters are cunning. As always, her worldbuilding is phenomenal. The imagery is absolutely stunning.However, if you are seeking a story that diverges from the author’s usual style or tropes, you will be disappointed. Two of the main characters are all but copied and pasted versions of two other beloved Grishaverse characters. The story of a young man and woman tiptoeing the edge of damnation? Sounds familiar. What started off as a very strong story took a nosedive in pacing about halfway through and just devolved into chaos. And that ending? I mean, I was rolling my eyes.Though this book had many of the author’s trademark style and dialogue, it ultimately lacked in chemistry between the characters and chemistry between the readers. I truly did not feel compelled to care about any of the characters or their fates. I felt like I was being held at arm’s length.The Familiar is the author’s first foray into historical fiction, and while fans may laud it as a success, I felt like it was a well-researched and immersive story that ultimately left its cardboard characters withering at the door.

The Familiarwas good, but nothing about it really wowed me. I enjoyed my time reading it, but it likely won’t be a standout or memorable book for me this year, sadly.I wish the setting was more prominent. If I didn’t know before starting this book that the story takes place in the 1600s during the Spanish Inquisition, I wouldn’t have been able to gather that information from the narrative. Maybe that’s just me being dumb though, because I have heard others mention the setting was a prominent feature.The entire book was rather slow-moving to me, and I do wish the pace had been faster. I felt the whole time I was reading that it was moving along very leisurely, and that frustrated me a bit. Especially when the plot picks up, the pace should too, but I personally feel that it did not.I felt rather emotionally distant from the entire story, including from the characters. All the characters outside of Luzia and Santángel fell flat for me, unfortunately, and I found myself not really caring what happened to any of them. I was most invested in Luzia of everyone.I really enjoyed Luzia as a protagonist though and thought she was deceptively strong-willed, which I love to see. She had a tiny bit of magic, which was cool too. Even though she had the ability to use some magic, this story definitely reads like a historical fiction and not like a fantasy though; the fantastical element is so small, found in just her tiny miracles and in the familiar’s immortality, but that's really it.I didn’t feel the chemistry between Luzia and Santángel at all. He seemed pretty creepy to me the whole novel, but love was clearly developing between them. When did he turn from the unsettling emaciated immortal creature to the handsome and loving man?I didn’t particularly care for Santángel as a love interest, but I do appreciate that Bardugo included a non-traditional love interest in this novel. I did enjoy learning about his backstory and why he is immortal though. In fact, that was the most captivating chapter of the whole book for me.The ending kind of came out of nowhere, and while I’m not sure yet if I liked it or not, I do appreciate it and the message it was communicating. I like that it wasn’t a conventional ending either, something both expected and unexpected at the same time.Maybe Leigh Bardugo’s writing style just isn’t for me. I have enjoyed the books I’ve read by her but I haven’t really loved any of them. I felt emotionally detached fromThe Familiarand from most of the characters, and I’m sad about that. I was prepared to love this book and have a great time reading it, but it was just a book that I read, no emotional strings attached, no significant impact on my life hereafter. I know many people are going to love this book though, and I wish I were one of those people too. It was fine, but that’s about it.I received a copy of this book for review from the publisher via Edelweiss.My Book Blog:Storeys of Stories

What the hell?I have a habit of not DNFing books, but every now and then, a story appears that seriously tests my resolve.The only way I can explain why this book has even made it to the stores is that sometimes, an author´s name is big enough that their book is published with no questions asked because it is a given that it will sell well. If an editor was even involved in creating The Familiar (which I highly doubt), they should be sacked on the spot.I don´t enjoy writing reviews like this, especially because Leigh Bardugo is one of my favourite authors, and especially because she said multiple times during the marketing campaign that the story holds personal significance to her. Unfortunately, I can honestly say I could not find a single redeeming quality that would change my mind.If I didn´t know The Familiar takes place in 16th century Spain from the blurb, nothing in the way this story is told makes it apparent to a reader. The language is far too contemporary and the way the characters interact with each other is in no way authentic.None of the characters are properly fleshed out, which means I didn´t connect with anyone enough to root for or against them. The romance is the absolute height of nauseating cliché tropes and it is completely unnecessary here. I was actually very surprised the author half-arsed it so badly because she usually nails the will they / won´t they tension perfectly.The pacing is completely off as well. The Familiaris a novel about people whowant: want what they can't have, want too much, want the wrong thing or the wrong person, want at the cost of something or someone else.It's a novel that explores what it is to want, that looks at wanting in its many inflections: longing, desire, lust, greed, gluttony, hunger.And there is much to be sought after inThe Familiar, whether material (food, dresses, comfortable beds, big houses) or not (power, agency, freedom, love). Every character inThe Familiardesperately and viscerally wants something, and what drives the novel's story is what they're willing to do to get what (or who) they want.But the matter of wanting very quickly transmutes into the matter of who gets to want in the first place, and whodeservesto get what they want.Our main character, Luzia, has lived her whole life feeling lesser than, told to hide her magic and her Jewish heritage. Her desire for a comfortable and luxurious life feels, to her, as though she is overreaching. Who is she to stray so far from what life has allotted for her? Who is she to want more than the existence she is eking out as a scullion for a careless and oftentimes cruel employer? On the flip side, we have the powerful men she is surrounded with, men who can conceive of no limit to what they want. Men who collect people as they collect things. The world is theirs for the taking; all they have to do is to go out and take it.Where does desire end and greed begin? When does wanting become wantingtoo much? These questions carry over well to a novel that's also grappling with the (very) tenuous line between faith and heresy, miracles and magic.And it's a line with devastating consequences: in an age of the Spanish Inquisition, any hint of heresy or "demonic" influence could possibly get you executed. Luzia is caught in the middle of all of this: she wants a life better than the one she would've ever had as a scullion, and yet the way to get to that life is through magic that could potentially be viewed as "demonic" or heretical. She is trying to take agency of her life, to actively work towards something greater, and yet she is caught up in the dangerous web of power and manipulation of the men around her, all of whom of course have their own motives and desires.Set during the Spanish Golden age,The Familiaris also very much grounded in a particular historical time and its attendant politics, laws, codes of conduct, etc. But as historically grounded as it is, it's also a novel that feels really timeless, one whose themes transcend its historical context--and one whose timelessness feels all the more fitting given that it's inspired by fairytales and is, itself, a kind of fairytale.Everyone knows what it is to want something, no matter how big or small, andThe Familiaris such a sympathetic and vital account of a woman with this bone-deep craving for more that she cannot let go of.And throughout it all, Bardugo's writing is so perfectly suited to this story: it just sweeps you up, vivid and enchanting even as it jolts you to the violent realities of its world.In the writing as in the narrative,The Familiarhas all the enchantment of a fairytale, with all the grit and bite of a story that sees the true cost of the fairytale story.

And then every now and then Bardugo would drop in some Alex Stern wannabe one-liners that felt completely out of place. The first quarter of the book almost feels like it’s setting up her villain origin story (which is most definitely the book I would have rather read) only for her to demure and wait for her boyfriend to guide and save her. Homegirl has seemingly endless magic as long as she can sing? Get the bitch some throat coat and start the rampage!And as for the love interest, he’s sold as some sexy demon. This man is not that. He’s a codependent vampire. Darlington he most certainly is not.His origin, told as a fairytale bedtime story, is the strongest part of this book. It’s a few paragraphs. The rest of the time he’s some impotent sad boy bemoaning the state of it all. My dude, you are literally immortal. Just wait Victor out. Better yet, seduce your masters? That’s the book I wanted to read.It’s another fantasy competition trope. It’s Hunger Games. It’s Throne of Glass. It’s the Jasad Heir. It’s damn similar to Miss Congeniality with the water glasses. Nothing about this book feels all that new. It has nothing insightful to say about religious persecution, in fact, it almost romanticizes it. Santangel is a vampire without actually being a vampire. He’s like oh no, I have to be Victor’s hitman. But like he literally doesn’t? He’s immortal with no earthly attachments. He could literally just wait him out.The side characters are pointless. We talked about this playwright for ages just for her to be a lesbian side romance that we spend all of two sentences on. For why? Diversity brownie points?None of the villains actually felt threatening. The couple’s happy ending felt too inevitable, so nothing felt like it had any stakes. We’re never invested in Luzia winning the competition because all we do is get told how it would still be awful if she did.I’ll allow that I’m probably not the target audience for this book. I don’t give a shit about history, and I know nothing about it. This book was name-dropping peoples, places, and things left and right and I have absolutely no clue who any of them are. Maybe they’re nice little Easter eggs if you’re that kind of nerd. The religious angle did nothing for me. I’m wildly anti-religion, so do with that what you will. Luzia doesn’t come across as particularly faithful anyway? So why was she even fighting so hard to hold onto something she doesn’t even believe in? And she doesn’t fight all that hard? She just wants to be a stay-at-home mom for her husband. But like she’s not even gonna get to do that? So like is it even really happily ever after?And said boyfriend really leaves so much to be desired. I am not a bully romance girlie. I can’t really come back from you thought she was stupid and ugly. You wanted to sell her into eternal servitude, but like you ate her coochie one time and now everything’s different? You literally need her to live? Codependency is just not for me.The Inquisition torture was a joke. They built it up as such an awful thing in the story, and you know it’s an awful thing from history, but then homegirl has unlimited healing magic, gets dunked in some water, and then sleeps it off. How is that threatening? How is that scary? Literally while she’s set to be burned alive, she’s thinking about how she can just heal herself, so it’ll be fine.This book was never horror. It was never the romance I wanted to read. It was another flop. I’m having such a bad reading year, and I worry that it’s souring me on my ratings a bit, but fuck me, I want more from these books!Who should read this:Addie LaRue girliesHistorical fantasy fansFantasy competition trope fansMagical realism girliesJewish but make it fantasy fans (did not think this was a sub-genre but this makes 4 books with this same flavor that I’ve read in the last six months.)Do I want to reread this:Nope.Similar books:* The Invisible Life of Addie LaRue by V. E. Schwab-historical magical realism, oh no, I made a deal with a demon and now I’m immortal and for some reason, I consider this a bad thing, lackluster romance* Jasad Heir by Sara Hashem-this book but a way better romance, ENEMIES to lovers, fantasy competition trope, religious persecution commentary* Throne of Glass by Sarah J. I have read all of Bardugo's books except for the sequel to The Ninth House as I did not like that book at all and to make a long story short, I love her books. I have shouted enough about Six of Crows that I got many friends into that series too. I was waiting for Bardugo's next book which is not in the Grishaverse so when the Familiar was announced I was happy and excited. I am a bit disappointed after finishing the book.To be honest, I was fair to the author as I went into this without any intention to compare it to her other books as it is a standalone novel. The problem is that after doing some reading and feeling underwhelmed, I automatically did those comparisons. Let's start with the writing, Bardugo's prose is great, and she has some epic lines that I know by heart. The Familiar felt like a debut novel instead of a latest novel. The writing was good but good is not enough when you know an author can write excellently. And here, I am taking a moment to praise the cover art which is good and even better and makes more sense when you read the story!Also, Grishaverse has some of the most memorable characters I ever read. Starting from the Shadow and Bone series to the Six of Crows and even including The Rule of Wolves. The characters in this book are so forgettable. The book is called The Familiar and I thought that that would be the protagonist but in fact, it is the antagonist, and our protagonist is a servant who does some small miracles with magic. I thought that Bardugo was trying to imitate the chemistry between The Darkling and Alina, but it just didn't work. I can't still decide if it was a YA novel or an adult novel or something lost in between.The story line was kind of interesting at first but then it moves slowly losing its momentum and becoming duller. I loved the story within the story which Bardugo does greatly in most of her books. I wanted to know more about the Familiar and his curse and it was the only thing that grabbed my interest in the story. The story is personal to Bardugo and reflects her family history including the not-nicest parts. I think the ending was okay and maybe it reflects this history, but I was expecting more.The soft magic system did not really impress me. I am usually a bigger fan of harder systems, but this definitely had more potential that was never reached. At the end of the day and despite me not wanting to make comparisons. Everything just worked better in her other books. I wish I could say this was better, but I am not convinced.So, this was not a bad book, but I know that Bardugo has so much more potential as a writer. Everything was "just okay" here and that is not enough when there are many great books to read out there. The writing was good, the characters, storyline and magic were less so. I still am a fan of Bardugo and still looking forward to her next work.

reviews.review_text: I’m having a hard time stringing thoughts together for this review. Mostly because I feel like I'm still processing a lot of what Bardugo did with this story. It's not quite a fairytale or a retelling but there are layers and meanings and messages within THE FAMILIAR and most, though they are dressed up in different ways and from different angles, come together to speak about the same thing : desire. Or, maybe more specifically, wishes and wanting. And we often see the results of those wishes and wants played out in fairytales; the unloved mistreated daughter who ends up in a castle. The powerless becoming the powerful. The dying becoming the immortal. And on and on. But rarely do we see the aftermath of those happily ever afters and whether there is a cost to their wanting to better their circumstances -- or it they are lucky enough to not live long enough to see their wishes become curses.There was pleasure in shared magic, and danger too. It pricked the mind and the spirit. It filled the room with possibility.Somehow this story is all those things. But it's also a lot more.Men weren't kind to the things they feared.Set during the Spanish Golden Age, there is a sharp edge hiding amongst the magic and miracles, comprised of fear and heresy, blasphemy and inquisition, greed and control. There is also loss, which we see so heartbreakingly played out through Luzia's eyes, that becomes transmuted, adapted, partly buried but not forgotten, and that's the loss of heritage, of culture, of identity, of language, all in the service of having to become something you're not just to survive. Of having to walk away, to stifle your grief instead of share it, time and time again, knowing no one would understand."Fear men, Luzia. Fear their ambition and the crimes they commit in its service. But don't fear magic or what you may do with it."But it's also about becoming -- and we see that play out with a few different characters as they discover who they really are and who they mean to be. There's also a romance that brings joy and wonder even as it means an ending. And, finally, there's sacrifice, and what's left when the endless run of luck finally, well, runs out.I found it hard to put this down and I definitely think it's going to stay with me for a while (RIP to my next read). But to those who are expecting lots of drama or big magical showdowns, don't. This is a quieter, slower, kind of read and, as I sit here, struggling to cobble together something that resembles a review, I'm perhaps left feeling more contemplative than effusive but I don't think that's a bad thing. Not at all.If you're a Bardugo stan, you likely need no convincing to give this a go. And for the rest, especially the historical fiction fans, I would definitely recommend you consider picking this one up.** I received an ARC from the publisher (thank you!) in exchange for an honest review. **---This review can also be found atA Take From Two Cities.

“Language creates possibility. Sometimes by being used. Sometimes by being kept secret.”My Spanish ass was intrigued by this historical fantasy novel from the moment I saw that it was set during the Spanish Golden Age. In addition toThe Familiarbeing one of my most anticipated releases of the year, it was also the first book I read by Leigh Bardugo outside of the Grishaverse. So let’s just say that there were a series of expectations before delving into this novel.The story starts off in late 16th century Madrid—the exact year isn’t mentioned, but we can deduce that it’s at the end of the century because that’s when Antonio Pérez tried to flee after falling out of favor with the king. We follow Luzia Cotado, a scullion in the Ordoños household who usesmilagritosby singingrefranesin Ladino. When she is discovered by the lady of the house, she finds herself entering a competition where se has to perform hermilagritosand avoid attracting too much attention so that no one suspects either her real powers or her Jewish ancestry. Guillén Santángel is the other main character, an immortal familiar who will have to train Luzia.Let’s get straight to the point: this story is nothing new. A girl has powers that she must hide, she meets an immortal boy and enters a magical tournament. A premise that I’ve read before and that, in this case, is quite linear and predictable. But still, it’s an entertaining story that is easy to read and told with a writing style that I really liked—you can tell how much it improved from the first books Bardugo published and it made me even more excited to check out her Alex Stern series.It seems that the author did her research before writing this novel, but although she made an effort to explain the convoluted political intricacies of the time and the persecution of the Jewish population by the Inquisition, the story could have been set in any other city due to the lack of descriptions and exterior locations—most of the story takes place indoors—so that aspect of the story was quite underwhelming.Summing up, I liked this novel but didn’t love it. The writing was definitely the star of the show for me and I enjoyed the romance, but both the setting and the plot were quite average. I also kind of liked the ending, except for the last couple of pages. An enjoyable read which doesn’t offer anything new to the genre but which I think many fans of the author will like.Instagram|Twitter

If I could sum this book up in two words, it would be:Wasted potentialI was so disappointed in my reading experience of The Familiar that I can barely comprehend it. The book had all the elements of making for a fantastic read. A girl taking back her agency. Romance with an immortal being (whom I thought for months before reading the book was a vampire, but I digress). Magic. Magic and its complicated relationship with religion. A very interesting historical setting. A magic tournament. But every single one of these elements fell short. And I mean every. single. one. of them.One of the things that attracted me to this book is its setting. Spain in the 1800s, which is a place and a time we barely see explored, or I personally, haven't read much about. But the author didn't manage to pull me in. The setting feels like watching a movie where the image is extremely unsaturated, the exposition turned all the way down that you can barely see anything going on. And you can TELL it's not an intentional stylistic choice. It all just gives an overwhelming feeling of... bleh.And don't get me started on the tournament. I am a huge fan of magical tournaments, and it took a HUGE chunk of this book, but at the same time it felt like I barely had a grasp of anything happening. There was barely any effort put into explaining or describing anything happening. The overwhelming feeling I got, was that the author just took a bunch of seller tropes, put them together into one story with barely surface level exploration and hoped for the best. It felt...lazy, and not at all what I had come to expect from Bardugo sadly.The romance was supposed to be this angsty, scandalous, forbidden thing but I could barely be convinced these two romantically LIKED each other, let alone that they would go to great lengths for one another. Where is the author who gave us the emblematic Kaz and Inej? Where was the off the charts tension those two offered us? Nowhere to be found, I'll tell you that much.Tldr: I was very apathetic and bored start to finish.

I expected the worst since I had issues with Hell Bent (too confusing), and the reviews for this weren't too kind (bad, boring, etc.).The Familar is a story about a heroine who is poor (a maid), has powers (the ability to change things to their original form if broken or ruined), and has a feisty streak (she comes to the point where she is pretty vocal about what she wants and who she is, and takes crap from no one). Her mistress discovers she has this power and from starting off as rich entertainment (doing little tricks for her mistresses' rich crowd) she is thrust into a competition for magic advisor to the king of Spain.Where does the Familiar come from? Santangel. You could say this is her story as much as it is hers. She is the catalyst, the cure for him. You see, Santangel has a predicament (which you find out) where he must serve as the magic being to a family. His owner / master has been trying to form a collection of other gifted magic users and when word of our lead hits him, he is roped in to be her tutor in her magic. If he succeeds he gains his freedom. So he wants to be freed, and badly, so he does this... but w know that things don't turn out that easy and romance of the heart is part of this.I liked that the plot was easy to understand, and I enjoyed the time period it took place in (also with the historical bits here and there). However, I felt that even though this is an adult fantasy (the characters have sex and they do swear), it had the formula of a YA. It wasn't as dense as Alex Stern, and that is a bit puzzling since given the historical background and history proclaimed in this you would want more of it. The world around them feels... flat at times? Like, you don't really grasp that they're in Spain, or there is the Inquisition going on (it's mentioned a lot). So I guess you can say that is the reason I rated it down a star.Since it is a stand alone, the story gets wrapped up by the end. There could be a sequel either with the lead and Santangel or new characters if Leigh chooses. All in all, I enjoyed it.

This story follows Luzia who is a scullion working in Madrid, she’s got these special powers that come to light and things kinda snowball from there.This book will hold a very special place in my heart for a very long time- it’s a story of finding your identity while being disconnected from your entire lineage. It’s a story of courage and longing for something MORE, something better; of a girl who deserves more and is ready to risk familiarity for a taste of it.I loved the 3rd person multiple POV format!! It flowed and really worked to enhance my understanding of the world and the characters; I’d go from actively disliking a character to pitying them, back to resenting them, to understanding why they are the way they are- a whole range of things were happening for almost every character. To be able to have readers committed to the personal developments of side characters- or any characters beyond the mains- is a real feat, and I’m not shocked that Leigh was the author to do it. One of my favourite things was that each and every character was fleshed out, developed, stood on their own. They had their own desires, fears, ambitions, beliefs, motivations, it was a real joy to see their developments across the story. I love that not every character’s story ended the way they deserved, or how I wanted or expected. Each ending felt so very real, so inevitable- not like an author created it but like these were real people’s lives being recounted through fiction. It was heartbreaking, and fulfilling, and devastating- the tears I was shedding were both joyous and sad.We were promised this was going to be her most romantic book yet, and was it? Absolutely. Without a doubt. Not just the romance between the main couple, but just as a story- it dealt with all the emotions- the ones that made the characters feel like they were floating and the ones that felt they could rot them from the inside out. It was visceral and enchanting and truly a credit to her skill in creating life from words. Seeing the grandeur of Spain from the POVs of VERY different characters w majorly different experiences was FANTASTIC!! I was completely captivated by the historical setting, the research and care that so obviously went into depicting this time period and the social/political/religious conditions. The blend of history with fiction was beautiful. There’s a line towards the end- something like ‘but who really knows what the king was thinking that day.’ And i think about that line A LOT!!! It kinda felt like the fourth wall was being broken- I was like OH okay she’s taking liberties and we’re in Philip’s head but then that line came and I was like OH okay this is why I will read anything and everything ms Bardugo writes okay cool let me just sit quietly here in the corner LMAO 😮‍💨😮‍💨😮‍💨😮‍💨I didn’t know what to expect since this is her first standalone and I really had to read the last pages multiple times over bc my eyes kept jumping around trying to see what came next. The resolution was PHENOMENAL. Second only to the emotional explorations pertinent to Luzia and Santángel, the resolution/comeuppance of certain characters and Luzia and her lover’s ending was my absolute favourite part. It was…. EVERYTHING. Did I expect a lil more punch towards the end? Yes. Would that have been best for the story? No. Both can be true; this was one hell of an ending. It was both devastating and also the most hopeful, beautiful thing I’ve ever read. I was sobbing but also laughing and feeling so many things because it wasn’t perfect but they made do and they deserved all those years. I love them so much 🥲😭♥️A stunningly raw, and enchantingly emotional account of love, ambition, and what it takes to reconnect with who you are, and discover who you want to be. I was completely enthralled from the very first page, to the very last.If you didn’t like any of her previous works, and you’re thinking about trying this one- do!! It stands so strongly as its own distinct piece of work and is deffo worth the read! ♥️Update: (04/04/24): thinking about how fascinating it was to watch Luzia confront her desire for more, be it material or quality of life or ambition, to see her face it head on and commit to it even if it would (and did) become her doom!!! The way she had made peace with it very early on- that she would see it through regardless of it it burned her, and to see she stick by that and see her be calm in the face of death was something incredible to read. Often we say one thing but when push comes to shove we back out etc, but not Luzia. Loved this detail so much. It’s a certain stubbornness that is both admirable and also makes my survival instinct SHAKE but either way,, she said what she was about and didn’t have to say it twice lolThank you Viking UK for the proof copy in exchange for an honest review !!

4.5/5Aboltar kazal, aboltar mazal.What an outstandingly beautiful book, I absolutely adored every second I spent reading it. Whilst it was phenomenally immersive and so wonderfully atmospheric, that never came at the sacrifice of the plot or the characters. Everything was littered with such beauty and meaning, every emotion was strung together to create a story that became mesmerising.What I love so much about Bardugo's adult novels is the trust she places in the reader, she entrusts us to pick apart the characters' actions and analyse the thematic components without ever beating us over the head with it or having to hold our hand from one point to the other. It makes for a remarkably subtle yet strong narrative, and deepens the characters in such a rich and compelling way.Fear men, Luzia. Fear their ambition and the crimes they commit in its service. But don't fear magic or what you may do with it.The characters are gifts. I love that Bardugo never backs down from unwieldy and flawed characters, it enlivens them greatly and makes them feel wholeheartedly real. Our main character, Luzia, became such an incredible protagonist. She has all the secret-keeping and forced humility of a servant, all the loneliness and humiliation that comes alongside that too, yet she is hungry. And then, all of a sudden, there is the opportunity to change her fortune, to lead a life full of radiant possibility, to clasp at power with both hands, and she decides she will take it. It doesn't matter if she should, it doesn't matter if she deserves it, it doesn't matter if it will thrust her into dangerous waters, it is what she desires. She wants nothing more than to be the one in control of her own future, to be the one at the helm of her own ship. But between the secret of her Jewish blood, the mysterious familiar with whispers of his own to hide, and the ones who would use her power for themselves, Luzia must contend with a world where one wrong footstep will send her straight into the Inquisition's cells. After all, the line between magic and heresy is very thin. Her small miracles can be construed as the work of God, but the words she uses will only condemn her.I adored how important language is in this story. Luzia is a scullion girl, she is not meant to know how to read, the only Latin she is meant to know is in the scraps of Catholic prayers. But Luzia's history is long and vast, full of people disguised and concealed, spread across lands and hidden in the shadows. And it is there that she finds the language of her magic. It is a culmination of many languages, some forbidden and some forgotten, words scavenged across time. It is all of these languages and it is none of them. It is a collection and a remembrance. And it is the source of her magic, these words that could ruin her but that make her who she is.Her refranes were Spanish and Hebrew and Turkish and Greek. They were none of those things. They changed depending on what part of the world the letter came from. They were words battered and blown to all corners of the map, then returned to her, as the people who spoke them could never return."No language," she snapped in frustration. "Every language."Luzia's relationships with everyone around her were complicated and fascinating, as they were all such intriguingly complex characters, and I couldn't help but love them all in their own ways.Santángel held such mystery and burning rage, his was a fire that fuelled much of the narrative and led down very interesting paths. They both inspired and stoked a hunger within one another, desiring the pomegranate taste of power and the bittersweet scent of freedom. I loved their dynamic and the layered trust that began to brew between them.Valentina was another who was compelling, a timid character comparatively, but one who wanted just as furiously. Her and Luzia's relationship was incredibly intricate, one that curved and grew into a vast array of flowers and thorns, never quite what you might have expected.But it was Hualit who absorbed me the most. She is a wholly flawed character who has had to fight for the small power she now wields, who has to bear every humiliation and every torment that others have desired, who must still bear it or yield to the anger of another commanding man. She knows the dangers of the court, she knows how to dance through the politics of the upper classes, she knows how to save her own skin. But it is precisely because of this, because she has always had to suffer to survive, that she will not share the burden of Luzia's suffering also. Theirs is a fraught and shifting dynamic; one of a shared and complicated grief, one of stone walls that cannot be scaled, one of a solitary understanding, one of a love that will not save them. It is Hualit, in her iron will, in her insightful fear, in her desperate glance at freedom, that best depicts Luzia's strange and heartfelt relationships.I would rather be a fool than a coward.Power, desire and freedom all play immense roles in the telling of this story. In my opinion, they are the strongest themes and shine fiercely at the forefront. They are scattered all throughout, in the actions of each character, in their flimsy wishes and last hopes, in the things they care for and all that they are willing to sacrifice. As I said before, Bardugo expertly handles them without having to spell it out for the reader and I think that makes them all the more captivating, the fact that you must dig for them and find the depths of what is said beneath. Bardugo intelligently cultivates all of these themes in very different ways within each of the characters; freedom is an eventuality Luzia seeks through gaining power, freedom is Santángel's most valued wish, freedom is a dream faded from Valentina's mind, and freedom is Hualit's sacred future. It is a story told in the separation and isolation of its characters that is then woven back together through the threads that bind Luzia to all its players.It is a beautiful book, written in such lush and elegant prose. It is often poignant, it is often melancholy, and it is often treacherous. We are swept away so effortlessly into the currents of history and become utterly absorbed in the pages. Every word I read drew me deeper and deeper into the past of Renaissance Spain, Bardugo easily enraptures us in this spell-binding and atmospheric tale. It is a book I never wanted to leave the pages of and of which I adored every last word.For my family—converts, exiles, and ghosts.As you can probably tell, I loved this book with all my heart. It's phenomenal thematic exploration, its exquisite prose, its all-encompassing atmosphere, its intricate and detailed characters, all made for a brilliant book that I am very excited to return to in the future. I adored it immensely!

I should have tempered my expectations after the fiasco that wasHell Bent. Bardugo seems to want to write this style of romantasy that appeals to the current market and is good for her, go make bread. But I'm afraid this isn't for me.Discussing my issues with the new style of Bardugo's work with a friend and I believe the issue is in how she tries to give these dues ex machine endings that end up being sickly perfect. These endings just do not work with the edgy and dark vibe she is going for in her stories. It ends up being unsatisfying and like too sweet cakes, mostly frosting and no flavor. Apart from my issues with the ending to this (which just FYI was just another rehashing of the S&B ending), I had issues with the simplicity of the plot and the characters. I kept waiting for that "oof" moment where I would be blown away by Bardugo's plotting (and I know she can be great at that, she wrote the Six of Crows books and Ninth House (no we are not mentioning Hell Bent in this house)) but it never happened and I just continued to be disappointed more and more with every chapter.The characters are bland and I am already forgetting them. Looking at all the 5 star reviews I’m not convinced I have read the same book as the rest of the internet.We follow a scullion who possesses a magic that allows her to accomplish her daily tasks more easily. When her mistress discovers her power she exploits her to rise in social favour and Luzia ends up in a magical tournament consisting of various trials. The aim is to win the king of Spain’s favour. The book takes place during the time of the Inquisition and having never studied this period I did enjoy the historical setting.I do, however, think this book has been marketed incorrectly. I was expecting a lush and intricate historical fantasy with rich world building and romance. Instead I felt the book was underdeveloped and certain elements of the plot felt very random.An overall issue I had was that Bardugo seemed very stingy with the character descriptions early on. We are constantly reminded that the protagonist is not like other girls, she’s just SO unattractive and plain, but I wanted more detail. I also found the magical change in Santangel’s appearance a bit random, I see what she was trying to do but going from corpse-like to a bang-able love interest felt jarring. The romance in general felt underwhelming and unwarranted. I barely felt any romantic tension. Also, Luzia has such big issues to deal with and the most pressing question is “can it be done against a door”.If I had a pound for every time the word pomegranate was used. Why has eating a pomegranate changed the protagonist’s life?? At what point did Bardugo’s pomegranate obsession begin? “She was the woman who had eaten the pomegranate” WHY is this meant to be so impressive. The pomegranates were just over done.The book obviously compelled me enough to keep reading. If I absolutely HATED it I would have DNF-ed. I was curious enough to see where the plot went and despite not being particularly emotionally connected to the characters I wanted to see what happened to them.I can absolutely recommend this to anyone trying to get into fantasy for the first time or exploring historical novels. However, for anyone well versed in those genres this book will most likely fall short of their expectations.Many thanks to the publisher for a copy in exchange for an honest review.

Dieser Wunsch nach mehr führt sie dazu, ihre Fähigkeit, kleine Wunder oder „Milagros“ zu vollbringen, zu nutzen, um der Plackerei ihres Alltags zu entfliehen. Damit begibt sich Luzia auf den Weg zu einem größeren, großartigeren Leben, als sie es sich je erhofft hätte - doch die jüdische Herkunft ihrer Fähigkeiten kann sie genauso schnell ihr Leben kosten.Guillén Santangel ist wie kein anderer auf der Erde, ein unsterblicher Vertrauter in den Diensten von Victor de Paredes, der für immer an die Familie de Paredes gebunden ist. Er existiert seit Hunderten von Jahren und das Leben bietet ihm keine Aufregung oder Interesse mehr – bis er Luzia begegnet. Während er ihr beibringt, wie sie ihre Kräfte erwecken und nutzen kann, kommen sie sich näher. Aber Santángel ist ein Mann mit vielen Geheimnissen, der gezwungen wurde, viele schreckliche Dinge zu tun, und sein Ruf als Mörder und Dämon ist für ihn und Luzia eine ebenso große Gefahr wie ihre eigene Gabe, Wunder zu vollbringen.Das Setting im Madrid des 16. Jahrhunderts hat mich genauso gefesselt wie die Charaktere und die Magie dieser Geschichte.Fazit:Der Vertraute hat mich mit einer unkonventionellen Liebesgeschichte, vielen tiefgründigen Charakteren, die ihre eigenen Ziele verfolgen und dem Spanien des 16. Jahrhunderts gefesselt.Ein Meisterwerk von Leigh Bardugo!

In Leigh Bardugo's historical fantasy novel,The Familiar, we are transported to the vibrant streets of 1500s Madrid during its golden age. Filled with political intrigue, religious tension, and a captivating love story, Bardugo presents a world teeming with vivid descriptions and three-dimensional characters. I loved the gorgeous pomegranates pictured on the end paper and the gothic looking book cover.The novel centers around Luzia Cotado, a young orphaned scullion maid working for Valentina and Marius Ordonio. Dona Valentina is an unkind mistress who discovers Luzia’smilagritas(miracles) and uses her to entertain guests as a way to gain popularity and better her social standing. Luzia’s only family is her Aunt Hualit (the widow or Catalina de Castro de Ono), who is Victor de Paredes’ mistress. Victor is a richcaballeroand the luckiest man, who convinces Luzia to enter a magic tournament for Antonio Perez, a disgraced former secretary to the king. Then there’s Guillen Santangel, Victor's servant (the familiar) who is assigned to train and prepare Luzia for the tournament. All these characters have stakes in Luzia winning the competition but who can Luzia trust??This was a well-paced story rich with Spanish culture and history. Bardugo demonstrates excellent plotting skills in creating a magical story within a true historical setting. The tension of the Spanish Inquisition adds an additional layer of unease, especially as Luzia conceals her Jewish identity.I appreciated the relationship between Luzia and Santangel, although I felt the romance developed a bit quickly. The dialogue between the two was fantastic, and the magical element of Luzia's power being drawn from songs was unique. Additionally, I enjoyed seeing Luzia’s character development and how her relationship with Valentina progressed.Overall, I enjoyedThe Familiarfor its rich portrayal of Spanish history and Bardugo's talent in creating a world filled with unique characters. It's a compelling read that seamlessly weaves together magic, history, and a dark fairy tale.

Actual rating: 3.5 stars, rounded up.The Familiarwas one of my most anticipated books of 2024. A dark, gothic, historical fantasy standalone written by an author I adore? Yes, please. I loved the idea of a story involving magic in Inquisition-era Spain, when there would have been such a thin tightrope to walk with that kind of gift. Bardugo does a wonderful job with her characters, and I expected this book to be no different in that regard. And yet, even thoughThe Familiardelivered on all of those expectations, I still found myself a bit disappointed in it. It’s quite possible that I picked it up at the wrong time, that I should have shelved it for later instead of muscling my way through it. Because it’s definitely a good book. Sadly, it simply didn’t land quite right for me.Let’s talk about the things that did work for me. First and foremost, the prose is gorgeous. Bardugo has always had a lovely way with words, but her craftsmanship just keeps improving. There were many sentences and passages that I found myself rereading, because they were just so pretty. She also managed to capture a very strong sense of time and place, both of which lent to the gothic air of the novel. I felt truly transported, even in sections that didn’t have as much physical description.Then there are the characters. Bardugo managed to craft a host of characters who all felt multifaceted. None were purely good, but few were without redeeming qualities. Luzia, our main character, is a surly scullion maid with illusions of grandeur and the power to back them up. I loved how unique she was, how brave and selfish she could be. Santangel, the man who helps her hone her gift, is enigmatic and absolutely fascinating. Even the side characters, like Valentina, Luzia’s employer, Haulit, her wealthy aunt, and Teoda, the Holy Child against whom Luzia competes to become the king’s champion, were very interesting.The Familiaralso provided a ton of food for thought. We are shown the religious rigors of the time, and how so much of religion was dictated by fear. We see the mistrust of all who are different, and how even conversion to Catholicism is not enough for a Jew or Muslim to earn the trust of the the government or its people. We see how people hide their heritage out of fear, suppressing large parts of who they are. And we see how, even when you follow every single rule to the letter, it is still not enough when an entity assumes as much power as the Spanish Inquisition.And now, onto the aspects that didn’t work as well for me. The pacing was my main issue. It was slow at times, nearly stationary at others. For a less than 400 page book, it felt like it had a tendency to drag. Frequently. It’s also a very political story. And I’m not big on politics, no matter the time or place. Finally, I expected the torneo determining which miracle worker would become the king’s champion to be a bit more exciting. While there were moments of magic and tension, it felt oddly mundane for a magical competition.Even thoughThe Familiardidn’t pack the punch I was hoping for, it’s still a very good book. Bardugo did a wonderful job with her characters, her setting, and the writing itself. I also really appreciated the ending; I though she really stuck the landing, so to speak. This is a book I look forward to rereading when I’m more in the mood for the darker, slower, more contemplative.

Já teda zírám, s čím byla Leigh Bardugo zase schopná přijít. Historická fantasy odehrávající se během španělského zlatého věku, mnohem vyzrálejší text, méně akční, spíš komorní, ale se skvělou atmosféru a nedokonalými hrdiny.Luzia Cotado je ta nejposlednější služka v domě chudého šlechtice a její život je plný dřiny, ponížení, je bez radosti a plánů do budoucna. Těžkou práci si usnadňuje používáním magie, kterou spolu se svým židovským původem skrývá, protože obojí se ve Španělsku trestá smrtí. Jenomže pak ji přistihne paní domu a začne Luzii využívat k pobavení hostů během honosných večeří, které si nemůže dovolit. A tam upoutá pozornost zavrženého bývalého tajemníka krále a Luzia začne se svou magií balancovat na hraně mezi pohodlným životem v luxusu a šibenicí, navíc pod dozorem nesmrtelného služebníka jejího patrona Guilléna Santangela (který je mimochodem takovým mixem Temnyje a Draca Malfoye).Neskutečně mě bavilo prostředí Madridu, kontrast mezi špinavými uličkami a honosnými paláci, celkově ponurá atmosféra a napětí budované zejména skrze všudypřítomné nebezpečí v podobě všech, kteří chtějí Luzii využít, kteří ji chtějí nahradit a kteří ji chtějí zabít. Vztah s Guillénem není pohádkový a všezachraňující, je postavený na tajemstvích a lžích, je zpočátku oportunistický, než se začne prohlubovat, je skutečnější. Thank you so much Penguin Books for sending me a free review copy of The Familiar!!Where do I even start with this book? I’ll be honest, when they first announced it, I didn’t really want to read the synopsis. I knew I was going to preorder and read it anyway so I wanted everything about it to be a surprise. I ended up going into this book knowing only that it was set during the Spain Golden Age when Philip II was the reigning monarch and I can honestly say I’m so glad that I went into this book blind.Ninth House was Leigh’s first venture into writing adult novels and it blew me away. The Familiar was no different despite how unique of a story it was, especially when comparing it to her previous works. It sits perfectly as a standalone and as much as I wanted more, I know deep down that I don’t need more because it was so perfectly planned. There may have been points where I was a little confused in regards to the scene or plot, but the majority of the time, it was cleared up. On the few occasions when they weren’t, it didn’t even bother because of how much the ambiguity matched the mysterious atmosphere of the book that at times felt like it was a character in itself in a way that I could not describe nor explain to you. It felt like a close friend who was guiding me through this magical tale.The multiple points of views was honestly so fun and it kept the pace going even when not too much was happening in those chapters. You still learned more about certain characters, or simply the history and backdrop of this book’s setting which I truly appreciated. Each of the characters felt so fleshed out and like real individual and complex people. You could dislike someone and in their next pov or even the next chapter that isn’t their pov chapter, you would pity them. Leigh loved to leave me feeling torn when it came to figuring out how I felt about each person which I found a very intriguing experience for myself.When she said that this book was her most romantic book yet, she was not lying. However, it wasn’t just the relationships between characters, particularly between Luzia and her love interest, but the writing itself and how it spoke about feelings and would at times leave me teary eyed. Without spoiling anything too much, I wish to mention that the romance between our protagonist and her lover was one full of tension, yearning and companionship that constantly left me feeling chocked up. Their banter and chemistry really jumps off the page from their first meeting and has you wanting more the entire time, which is honestly so fitting when it comes to them both as characters.By the end of this book, I was left feeling panicked and incredibly fearful of how she would end the novel. This being her only standalone, and so not knowing if she would leave us with a heart shattering ending or a joyous one, really upped the stakes in a way that I hadn’t expected.There isn’t much else to say that doesn’t start to spoil anything, so I highly suggest you go and preorder the book if you haven’t already, you won’t regret it.

Wow. What can I say? “The Familiar” was a lot in the best way possible. This book was my first introduction to the beloved author, Leigh Bardugo. I feel like when one is an active part of any social media, this name definitely rings a bell, regardless of whether one is a reader or not. Going into “The Familiar,” my hopes and expectations were set high, considering that the genre (historical fiction with elements of magic and supernatural set in 16th-century Europe) is my preferred and, of course, the author's popularity. It is pretty much obvious from my rating, that this book did not let me down in the slightest, and in this review, I would like to share all the things that made me love it so much.Starting off strong with Bardugo’s atmospheric, clever, and dark writing. I don’t usually annotate any of my books, but with this one, the amount of masterfully crafted sentences that almost made me forget how to breathe (no exaggeration here, whatsoever) was too much of a temptation not to turn my paperback into a rainbow of colourful sticky notes at its edges.Also worth noting, in my opinion, are the bonds between the three female characters in this book, which gave me, as a contemporary reader, a perspective on what the lives of women in different stages of life and social status look like. Hualit, Valentina, and Luzia, regardless of their initial dislike (this isn’t really a word that can describe their feelings towards each other, and I doubt the suiting word even exists; the situation was that complicated), still stood by each other’s side in situations of crises, being united by the simple fact of sharing a gender along with the feeling of longing for a better life. Too much, in a good way.“ What difference did it make if the person with the power wasn’t you?”

This took a little bit to get going, but once it did, I was not able to put it down until I finished it. I loved this book from beginning to end and I just didn't want it to end. I thought Bardugo's writing and just lyricism with certain words was fantastic. And this book did a great job of blending history, fantasy, and religion together."The Familiar" follows Luzia Cotado, a scullion living in Madrid during Spain's "Golden Age." Luzia has dreams though she knows they are impossible. Luzia though has a secret, she is able to "sing" and that seems to affect the things around her. When the mistress of her house, Valentina Ordoño figures out Luzia's secret, she is forced to perform for guests. Though Luzia knows what she is doing is dangerous, and if anyone finds out she could be tortured and deemed a heretic. When Luzia captures the attention of her aunt's patron, Victor De Paredes though, she realizes she is about to be forced to enter a dangerous game.I thought Luzia was fantastic. At first you may not like her, but she grows on you. Why shouldn't she dream of a bed, good food, and wine. Why should she be hiding herself away. She wants to take her gift and try to gain the notice of the king and in her eyes freedom. I maybe yelled a few times though because I thought she was being foolish. There's a secret to Luzia's magic and parts of it are linked to the forced conversion of she and her family from their Jewish religion to Christianity.I also really felt for De Paredes man/familiar named Santangel who is doing his best to not become attached to Luzia, but finds himself unable to leave her alone. I thought their growing attraction and love for each other felt organic to the story.The other characters we get to know, Luzia's aunt, Hualit Cana, Valentina, the other women/and one man that Luzia is up against, all come together nicely in this book.I thought the overall plot worked, but yeah, some parts did drag a bit at the beginning. But honestly, it did not bother me much because so many parts of the book were so good, I just wanted to go back and reread certain passages again and again.The setting of this book is during Spain's Golden Age which started when Columbus sailed the Ocean blue and ended around 1681. This book though is mostly focused around the 1580s during King Phillip II's rule and England rule under Queen Elizabeth I. I don't know how much readers know about it, but I don't think I have read a book set during that time and place (that was not a history book). Though it was called the "Golden Age" Spain would about expelling Muslim and Jewish people from their kingdom and did forced conversion to all to Christianity. We get historical characters such as these and Phillip's secretary, Antonio Perez he was fascinating (historically) and I liked how Bardugo portrayed him in this book.I really enjoyed the ending and will definitely seek this one out to buy for my permanent bookshelves.
