Forse se fosse nata in un giorno diverso, o almeno in un'ora diversa, senza le preghiere per l'anima di una regina che le riecheggiavano nelle orecchie, avrebbe potuto farlo. Ma non poteva che essere se stessa.Di solito scrivo le recensioni quasi subito, di pancia. Ma stavolta mi sono presa un giorno interno di decompressione prima di iniziare la lettura successiva, tanto ero rimasta connessa a questo libro anche dopo averlo chiuso.Aveva pensato che la paura rendesse la vita interessante? Ma non conosceva ancora la vera paura, giusto? Aveva assaggiato le spezie e le aveva trovate piacevoli. Ora stava masticando pepe, semi e tutto il resto.Dimenticate la Bardugo dei fantasy YA e delle ispirazioni russo/slave, dimenticate anche il ritmo di serie tutte colpi di scena e che possono permettersi di essere più leggere, in quanto basate su una base fantastica.Qui l'autrice parte da un contesto storico realistico, ovvero la Spagna di fine Cinquecento, provata e umiliata dopo lo sbaraglio dell'Invicibile Armada, con un re morente di gotta e una corte che si contende i suoi favori, mentre il potere religioso governa nell'ombra, tra condanne, roghi e torture. Se già di per sé il momento non è buono, la situazione più terribile la patisce chi viene sospettato di eresia o addirittura di essere un converso, un ebreo convertito a forza e che magari di nascosto tenta di preservare le proprie tradizioni.In un clima cupo e opprimente (sembra quasi di percepire dentro le pagine i miasmi di una Madrid sporca e infetta) l'orfana Luzia si barcamena come sguattera, occultando le sue conoscenze linguistiche, la sua intelligenza e i suoi doni legati a parole e saperi millenari. L'unica parente che le rimane è una zia, che cerca a sua volta di sopravvivere come amante di un uomo facoltoso.Ma sarà proprio questa conoscenza, in realtà, a dare il via a tutto.Per quanto in bilico tra fanatismo e tentazioni oscure, la corte iberica è affascinata da tutto ciò che sa di miracoloso, e ci sono uomini che vanno alla costante ricerca di talismani e di creature che riescano a modellare il fato e la fortuna, finché anche Luzia finisce nella loro rete.Si procede lenti, con un sottofondo malinconico costante, ma alla fine è quasi ipnotico, e avevo il terrore di andare avanti perché non ero sicura di sopportare cattive notizie su Luzia e lo Scorpione. Tuttavia è stata una storia molto bella, originale e profonda, in cui ho segnato tantissime frasi, seminate qua e là, come pietre preziose in uno scrigno.Triste e sublime.Ma sbagli a dire che non hai bisogno delle parole. Ne hai bisogno. Proprio come ne ha avuto bisogno Dio quando ha messo in moto il suo triste orologio. Le lingue creano possibilità. A volte nell'essere usate. A volte nell'essere tenute segrete.

I'll preface this with I don't know what god, saint, devil, or gentleman demon I have to thank for winning an ARC of The Familiar.This takes place in the Spanish Golden Age during a time of political and religious intensity. It follows Luzia, a servant with unique abilities. Once the household she works for finds out, they force her to use her gifts to partake in a competition to win the favor of Madrid's most influential people. An immortal familiar, Guillén Santángel is appointed to help her. While she manages to hide her Jewish bloodline and navigate the political minefield, there are many twists, turns, and mysteries!Luzia is a character that at first introduction seems meek or small. And one could say that's exactly how she wants to be seen. But even in those first pages, she is defiant. She is strong willed, a dreamer, and a fighter. Her character development is one of my favorite parts of this book. Her wit and determination is something you want to consistently root for.The historical setting feels so vivid and perfectly suited for the events and characters. It also has multiple third person POVs which adds a lot of insight and context throughout. Even for side characters, I just think it adds even more depth to the plot without adding confusion like some POVs can do. The story sheds a lot of light to social and power dynamics, privilege, and the Spanish Inquisition. There's a constant demonstration of privilege, poverty, and the dangers of having opposing religion or beliefs.I'll say it's different from what Leigh Bardugo has written but yet so many elements we're familiar with. There are characters we root for and then hate. Characters we dislike just to find ourselves understanding them or loving them by the end. It's something you get transported into and keep turning the pages for more. As with most of her stories, there is grit, hardships, and injustice. But there's also underdogs, survivors, and magic. I'll read anything she writes and this is no different 🫡And of course, Santángel. I promise not to spoil anything but I think everyone will love the broody, "evil", immortal, and morally grey love interest. He gives off a major "shouldn't fall for the girl but does anyway" but also "would burn for her".It's also a standalone so there's no cliffhangers but I feel like it had the perfect ending. Even though I was stressing until the very last pages lolol. 🥲 Usually I just scream about books rather than putting a full review together but overall, I cannot wait for everyone to read this and get my copy when it comes out!

I did it. I finished it before the publish date (thanks Edelweiss and Flatiron Books for the ARC)!4.5 stars, rounded up. It is honestly so refreshing to read a historical fiction set during the Spanish Inquisition simply because I rarely see it. I honestly learned so much. This story is so original, with it's very specific main characters. This is not a vampire story, which is what I might have assumed the flavor would be when reading "immortal" in the synopsis. And our protagonist is not just another unassuming girl who learns she is *special* either. I love our protagonist, Luiza, and her ambition. She is clever and works hard and knows what it means to fail, if and when she does fail. And if there's anything I love more than an ambitious protagonist, it's a creatively written and unfathomably ruthless villain. While there are no spoilers, I do wish that I got a little *more* of our antagonist doing antagonistic things, but really, the SPANISH INQUISITION does a lot of the antagonizing on its own. Absolutely worth the read. I may as well buy this sucker in hardcover, too, when it comes out, just to *hold* it.

I’ve read a bit of historical fiction about England in this same time frame, it was an interesting change to get a Spanish perspective.I overall really enjoyed this story. He was by far the most interesting character, and he ended up being kind of a flat romantic lead.

This kind of felt like reading a fable or Greek mythology. A slow read, but there was just enough mystery that kept revealing itself to keep things interesting. I thoroughly enjoyed reading and learning about these characters, but I found myself not caring much about the competition which makes up most of this book.

I quite liked Valentina as she had some good character development, but we didn’t have very much of her pov. Luzia was an attempt at a strong female protagonist- at a time where women should be quiet and meek she had some moments of strength but overall I didn’t warm to her.The love story also did very little for me, I found it hard to even visualise the male love interest (I feel like there were quite few physical descriptions in this book?) and their relationship wasn’t really fleshed out.Now the ending- I actually really liked the ending but it did feel rushed. The whole climax/plot twist end was crammed into about 20 pages which took me by surprise. It was a really good ending though and brought the book up in my estimations.Overall I would still recommend this as a creative, unique tale with a relatively well done gritty historical atmosphere, it just didn’t quite live up to my expectations.

People forget the work it takes to make wine. They drink it down and wonder why the cup is empty.A very frustrating experience, because of, I think, the slowness in the beginning and how the main character of Lucia just didn't feel engaging (to me). She didn't feel specific enough, an apparent scullery maid who actually knew latin and guess what? had a lot of power. In a way, the first part of her journey felt very Alina Starkov of Shadow & Bone. And then the book picks up at around 60% and it has some absolutely *great* moments, but it felt like too late for me.A think that struck me about this is the moments Bardugo chose to skip over and not show, not have us be present in... There were plenty of times where I felt like something was missing. And that the larger beats of the story and of the characters' growth were really lovely, actually, but they didn't really flow for me.Same with the romance. It had some suuuuper nice moments, but some of the connecting tissue was missing for me in that. Like when he says that he would spend an eternity unbraiding her hair - I loved that. But the relationship didn't feel real to me.Also, the whole inquisition aspect didn't feel like a real tense thing for most of the book, so I lost that emotional involvement I needed. The historical details were otherwise pretty great, but - how many times can I say it? - something felt like it was missing.What did surprise me was the evolution of abusive boss Valentina (even if I didn't buy it fully, see previous points). I also really enjoyed the playwright as a character. Otherwise, some of the plot points felt very tropey to me and expected.Like Lucia being convinced that her boyfriend is evil and is fooling her. That is such a trope and it annoyed the shit out of me when it happened, because I never bought into it.In the end, this was alright, looking forward to the next Bardugo book, since I've read most of them.18/31 reads in 31 days in January.

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐Pues que agradable sorpresa ha sido este libro.Empecé porque me llamó la atención la premisa de fantasía histórica además ambientado en España. En el pasado había leído mucha histórica y era una buena forma de volver a este género pero además con su toque de fantasioso. (Y que sin saberlo se convierte en lo que casi casi catalogaría como romantsy)La verdad que engancha mucho desde el principio y siempre tienes ganas de saber que va a ocurrir, aunque para mi gusto llega un punto que el libro se estanca un poquito sobre la mitad o un poco mas entonces empieza la recta final en la cual simplemente no podía parar de leer.Sistema de magia muy simple pero que cumple su función y pega bastante con el contexto y la época, y como se cruza con la religión y brujería. Así que por otro lado muy buen libro para personas que no están acostumbradas a leer fantasía como puerta de entrada al género.Cuenta también con la aparición de personajes históricos reales con cierta participación importante en la historia, lo que le da un punto extra de verosimilitud. Al mismo tiempo no necesitas saber mucho de historia para disfrutarlo y tampoco gira el argumento sobre acontecimientos reales, ni es súper preciso con fechas, etc. A mi me encanta la historia, pero si eres una persona que tiene cero interés lo vas a disfrutar igual y no te vas a perder en ningún momento, ya que se centra en los protagonistas y su historia particular, que evidentemente, es ficción.Por otro lado, mi grandísima sorpresa como he dicho al principio es como el libro por sorpresa se convirtió en casi un romantsy. El romance tiene un peso importante en el libro, y a mas avanza mas peso tiene y determina totalmente el destino y decisiones de los personajes. Me ha gustado bastante la relación entre los dos protagonistas, su dinámica y como evoluciona. Como dos personas "raras" que se acaban entendiendo, y como al final se puede encontrar a la persona adecuada.Recomendado 100%, una de mis mejores lecturas en lo que va de año. Una combinación perfecta de histórica, fantasía y romance

Da ich Leigh Bardugos Grisha-Verse liebe, war ich einerseits super gespannt darauf, was sie abseits des Bekannten erschaffen kann und hatte gleichzeitig Angst, dass es mir gar nicht gefallen könnte (diese Sorge wurde auch durch eher durchwachsene Rezensionen untermauert).Aber ich habe es geliebt! Aber ich verstehe auch, dass es viele nicht so gern mochten. Es ist eine etwas andere Geschichte. Eine einzigartige Geschichte. Der Vibe erinnerte mich ein wenig an eine Mischung aus "Die Tochter des Doktor Moreau" und "Das unsichtbare Leben der Addie LaRue".Das Buch lässt sich schwierig einem Genre zuordnen würde ich sagen. Ja es hat fantastische Elemente, aber diese stehen nicht exzessiv im Vordergrund. Ja es hat historische Elemente, aber auch das trägt mehr zur Atmosphäre als zu eigentlich Handlung bei. Apropos Handlung: ich bin im Nachhinein überrascht wie viel eigentlich in diesem Einzelband passiert ist, wie viele Personen und ihre Schicksale wir hier begleitet haben, während mir die Geschichte aber während des Lesens eher ruhig vorkam. Es gab keine großen Höhepunkte oder Plottwists, was allerdings grade dafür gesorgt hat, dass ich immer weiterlesen wollte und wissen wollte, was als noch alles passiert.Man bekommt die Geschichte von Luzia und dem Vertrauten nicht bloß aus einer Perspektive erzählt, sondern auch ganz vielen. Das war die ersten paar Kapitel zugegebenermaßen gewöhnungsbedürftig, aber nach einer gewissen Eingewöhnungsphase so cool und hat zusätzlich dazu gesorgt, dass ich an den Seiten geklebt habe.Ich könnte noch wirklich einiges zu diesem Buch sagen oder erzählen, möchte aber jedem die Chance geben so unbedarft an diese atmosphärische wundervolle Geschichte heranzugehen wie ich es getan habe. Das einzige was ich also sagen kann ist: wenn euch z.B. die oben erwähnten Bücher gefallen haben: traut euch, ich denke "Der Vertraute" könnte euch dann auch gefallen! :)

“In the darkness, all is one.”"The Familiar" is a quietly perseverant tale that delves into themes of suffering, resilience, and the struggle to find one's voice in a world that demands your silence. Set against a backdrop that seamlessly blends historical fiction with elements of fantasy, Bardugo crafts a narrative that hits all the right notes.At its heart, the story follows Luzia, a character who serves as a vessel for exploring complex themes like religious persecution, oppressive class systems, and the struggle for survival in a world you aren’t welcome in. Interwoven with this is a poignant romance that adds a welcomed depth to the story. Bardugo's writing skillfully maintains a delicate balance between sophistication and accessibility, rendering the novel both engaging and thought-provoking.Overall, "The Familiar" is a captivating read that combines historical depth with fantastical elements, offering readers a rich tapestry of characters and themes to explore. It’s a slow build, but one worth seeing to the end.

Leigh Bardugo’s The Familiar completely enchanted me—I couldn’t put it down! From the very first words, it felt like the book cast a spell, pulling me into its world. The setting was what hooked me first : I love stories with old Italian settings (Navola was one of my favorites this year, too), and Bardugo absolutely nailed the ambiance here. Her writing was so poetic and lush that I felt like I was there—the scents, the light, the portraits, even the textures of the draperies all felt so vivid and real.The characters, though, were what truly made this book shine. Luzia was everything. I loved her unapologetic nature—she’s a woman who isn’t afraid to say I WANT MORE from life, and I adored her for it. Santangel was also a fascinating character! Bardugo did such a great job capturing what immortality might actually feel like for someone like him, wasting away in boredom and servitude. It was so well done and so interesting. Their love was Perfection (with a capital P). It wasn’t one of those insta-love situations (which I can’t stand); it built slowly and naturally, which made it so much more satisfying.I also have to mention Valentina. I expected her to be the stereotypical cruel employer, but she wasn’t at all. She was layered, nuanced, and just as compelling as the rest of the cast. Honestly, all the characters were full of surprises—they felt raw, real, and completely different from what I expected in the best way possible.The plot was just as strong. I’m not usually a fan of competition tropes, but it was woven into the story so well here. It didn’t overwhelm the characters or the setting; it just fit perfectly. And that ending... it was so beautiful and heartbreaking that I actually cried, which almost never happens.I recommend this book. A lot!

**this honest review is based on an arc**This standalone started out strong and felt at first original, but alas it began to drag in the middle and that’s when all my attention was lost. Bardugo writes the most interesting secondary and side characters, and yet, from my personal opinion, always fail to get the MC to rise up to their potential. Santangel is a character with deeply amazing history and by far has the best dialogue, and Luzia, the protagonist, is just there. Most of the time she is bland and then at random points—to make plot happen—she’ll suddenly have a surge of out-of-character motivation that was not planted there before. I’m not convinced of their romance either. Bardugo is great with painting a moody backdrop and her writing has greatly improved with detailed (but concise) paragraphs, but her protagonists have not yet captured me. Instead of characters and plot being equal in their importance to allow a smooth-telling story, characters here are to serve the plot to be forced a certain way, which reads unnatural.
